--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reduce to one variable

Put  

\[
y=\sin ^2x\in[0,1]\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \cos ^2x=1-y .
\]

Then \(\sin ^4x=y^{2},\; \cos ^4x=(1-y)^{2}\) and  

\[
F(x)=f(y)=\sqrt{a+y^{2}}+\sqrt{b+(1-y)^{2}},\qquad 0\le y\le 1 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A lower bound (Minkowski’s inequality)

Write each term as a Euclidean norm in \(\mathbb R^{2}\):

\[
\sqrt{a+y^{2}}=\big\| (y,\sqrt a)\big\| ,\qquad   
\sqrt{b+(1-y)^{2}}=\big\|(1-y,\sqrt b)\big\|.
\]

Minkowski’s inequality gives  

\[
\big\|(y,\sqrt a)\big\|+\big\|(1-y,\sqrt b)\big\|
      \ge\big\|(y, \sqrt a)+(1-y,\sqrt b)\big\|
      =\sqrt{1^{2}+(\sqrt a+\sqrt b)^{2}} .
\]

Hence

\[
f(y)\ge \sqrt{1+(\sqrt a+\sqrt b)^{2}} .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  When does equality hold?

Equality in Minkowski occurs exactly when the two vectors are parallel and point in the same direction, i.e.

\[
\frac{y}{\sqrt a}= \frac{1-y}{\sqrt b}\; \Longrightarrow\;
y\sqrt b=(1-y)\sqrt a .
\]

Thus  

\[
y=\frac{\sqrt a}{\sqrt a+\sqrt b},\qquad 
1-y=\frac{\sqrt b}{\sqrt a+\sqrt b},
\]

which indeed belongs to \([0,1]\).  
Choosing any \(x\) with \(\sin^{2}x=y\) (such an \(x\) exists because
\(0<y<1\)) we obtain equality in (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Minimum value

Since the bound (1) is attained, it is the global minimum. Therefore  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\min_{x\in\mathbb R}\big(\sqrt{a+\sin ^4x}+\sqrt{b+\cos ^4x}\big)
      =\sqrt{(\sqrt a+\sqrt b)^{2}+1}
      =\sqrt{a+b+2\sqrt{ab}+1}\; } .
\]

The minimum is attained for any \(x\) satisfying  

\[
\sin^2x=\frac{\sqrt a}{\sqrt a+\sqrt b},\qquad 
\cos^2x=\frac{\sqrt b}{\sqrt a+\sqrt b}.
\]<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>
